'''''Eucalyptus conferruminata''''', commonly known as '''Bald Island marlock''' or '''bushy yate''',<ref name=anp>{{cite web|url=http://www.australianplants.com/plants.aspx?id=1007|title=''Eucalyptus conferruminata''|access-date=22 December 2017|publisher=Australian Native Plants}}</ref> is a small tree or [[mallee (habit)|mallee]] [[endemism|endemic]] to the south coast of [[Western Australia]]. It has smooth whitish and grey bark, elliptic to oblong or egg-shaped adult leaves, flower buds in fused in groups of between fifteen and twenty one, green to yellowish flowers and fruit forming a woody mass.

==Description==
This mallee or tree typically grows to a height of {{convert|2|to|8|m|ft|0}} and has smooth, grey and whitish bark and a bushy habit. Adult leaves are elliptical to oblong or egg-shaped, {{cvt|40-90|mm}} long, {{cvt|10-30|mm}} wide and the same glossy, light green colour on both surfaces. The flower buds are arranged in groups of between fifteen and twenty one or more in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s on a broad, strap-like [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|30-70|mm}} long. The buds are fused at the [[hypanthium]] with only the upper part free. The combined length of the fused hypanthia and each [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]] is about {{cvt|30-45|mm}}. The operculum is horn-shaped and about four to six times the length of the fused hypanthia. Green to yellow-green flowers appear from late winter to late spring between August and November. The fruit are fused to form a woody mass {{cvt|14-26|mm}} wide with three valves extending beyond the rim but remaining fused at their tips. The seeds are blackish brown with a flattened-ovoid to cuboid shape and are released through the gap between the valves.<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus conferruminata'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_conferruminata_subsp._conferruminata.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=4 June 2020}}</ref><ref name=vic/><ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|name=''Eucalyptus conferruminata''|id=5597}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus conferruminata'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20conferruminata |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=3 May 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The species was first formally described by the [[botanist]]s [[Denis John Carr]] and [[Stella Grace Maisie Carr]] in 1981 and the description was published in the ''[[Australian Journal of Botany]]''. The [[Type (biology)|type]] specimen was collected by [[Alex George (botanist)|Alex George]] on Middle Mount Barren in 1970.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus conferruminata''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/456014 |publisher=APNI|access-date=3 May 2019}}</ref><ref name="AJB">{{cite journal |last1=Carr |first1=Denis John |last2=Carr |first2=Stella Grace Maisie |title=The Lehmannianae: a Natural Group of Western Australian Eucalypts |journal=Australian Journal of Botany |date=1980 |volume=28 |issue=6 |page=535 |doi=10.1071/BT9800523}}</ref> The [[Botanical nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''conferruminata'') is from the [[Latin]] ''conferruminatus'' meaning "fused", referring to the fused buds and fruit.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="Sharr">{{cite book |author=Francis Aubie Sharr |author-link=Francis Aubie Sharr |title=Western Australian Plant Names and their Meanings |date=2019 |publisher=Four Gables Press |location=Kardinya, Western Australia |isbn=978-0-9580341-8-0 |page=168}}</ref>

In 2008, [[Dean Nicolle]], [[Malcolm E. French|Malcolm French]] and [[Nathan K. McQuoid|Nathan McQuoid]] described two subspecies of ''E. conferruminata'' and the names have been accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]]:
* ''Eucalyptus conferruminata'' <small>D.J.Carr & S.G.M.Carr</small> subsp. ''conferruminata''<ref name=APC1>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus conferruminata'' subsp. ''conferruminata''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/203857|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=3 May 2019}}</ref> that has an operculum more than {{cvt|12|mm}} wide at the base;<ref name="Nuytsia">{{cite journal |last1=Nicolle |first1=Dean |last2=French |first2=Malcolm E. |last3=McQuoid |first3=Nathan K. |title=A revision of ''Eucalyptus'' ser. ''Cornutae'' subser. ''Conjunctae'' (Myrtaceae) from the south coast of Western Australia, including the description of four new taxa and comments on the hybrid origin of ''E. bennettiae'' |journal=Nuytsia |date=2008 |volume=18 |pages=199–205 |url=https://florabase.dpaw.wa.gov.au/science/nuytsia/531.pdf |access-date=3 May 2019}}</ref>
* ''Eucalyptus conferruminata'' subsp. ''recherche'' <small>D.Nicolle & M.E.French</small><ref name=APC2>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus conferruminata'' subsp. ''recherche''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/214299|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=3 May 2019}}</ref> that has an operculum less than {{cvt|12|mm}} wide at the base.<ref name="Nuytsia" />

''E. conferruminata'' belongs in Eucalyptus subgenus ''Symphyomyrtus'' section ''Bisectae'' subsection ''Hadrotes'' because the coarsely bisected cotyledons, erect stamens and larger thick rimmed fruits. The subsection ''Hadrotes'' contains ten species of which eight do not have oil glands in the branchlet pith. Together these eight species form series ''Lehmannianae'', a group that have fruit with exserted valves that have fused tips even after the seeds are lost, a feature also shared with the distantly related ''[[Eucalyptus cornuta]]''.<ref name="CANBR" />

Of the eight species in series ''Lehmannianae'' four species, ''E. conferruminata'', ''[[Eucalyptus lehmannii|E. lehmannii]]'', ''[[Eucalyptus mcquoidii|E. mcquoidii]]'' and ''[[Eucalyptus arborella|E. arborella]]'' all have the buds in an axillary cluster that is fused basally.<ref name="CANBR" />

==Distribution==
Native distribution is limited to the south of [[Western Australia]], from [[Two Peoples Bay Nature Reserve|Two Peoples Bay]] east to beyond [[Esperance, Western Australia|Esperance]], including islands in the [[Archipelago of the Recherche]]. It is always found in coastal areas, often on massive [[granite]] rocks.<ref name=euc>Brooker, I. & Kleinig, D., ''Eucalyptus, An illustrated guide to identification'', Reed Books, Melbourne, 1996</ref> It is often found on hillsides and in gullies growing in sandy-loamy soils over granite or [[quartzite]].<ref name=FloraBase/>

The species has become naturalised in other parts of the Southwest region of Western Australia, via revegetation projects, windbreaks, and as a garden escapee.<ref name=FloraBase/> ''E. conferruminata'' has a limited distribution in [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] where it has become sparingly established in the [[Gippsland]] and [[Wimmera]] areas after having spread by seed dispersal from planted trees.<ref name=vic>{{cite web|url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/3f96afd6-65fa-4250-ace5-f0077b25af2a|title=''Eucalyptus conferruminata'' D.J.Carr & S.G.M.Carr|work=VicFlora|access-date=22 December 2017|publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria]]}}</ref> The species, once sold as ''Eucalyptus lehmannii'', has also become naturalised in California.<ref name="stanford">{{cite web |last1=Bracewell |first1=Ronald |last2=Rawlings |first2=John |title=''Eucalyptus lehmannii'', bushy yate · ''E. conferruminata'', bald island marlock {{!}} Trees of Stanford & Environs |url=https://trees.stanford.edu/ENCYC/EUCleh.htm |website=trees.stanford.edu |access-date=27 June 2018 |language=en}}</ref>

The subspecies most commonly cultivated in coastal regions of southern Australia, including in metropolitan areas of Perth and Adelaide is subspecies ''recherche''. Subspecies ''conferruminata'' is endemic to the [[Recherche Archipelago]] and does not occur naturally on the mainland.<ref name="Nuytsia" />

==Use in horticulture==
The plant is sold commercially as an ornamental, wind break or for [[erosion control]]. It will tolerate [[drought]] once established, moderate frost and grows in a variety of soil types including waterlogged soils.<ref name=anp/>
